prompt: Before this lesson, where was shelf's contract written?
hint: Every API has one, written down or not.

choices.text: Nowhere, because an API has no contract until somebody writes a document for it
choices.why: The contract existed the moment clients could depend on the answers; what was missing was a copy a program could read.

choices.text: In shelf.db
choices.why: The database holds the rows. The addresses, methods and status codes are not in it.

choices.text: In the code of rest.py, as the behaviour it produces
choices.why: Right. Addresses, methods, fields and codes were all fixed by rest.py, and reading Python or sending requests was the only way to learn them.

choices.text: In the HTTP standard, which defines what every API answers
choices.why: HTTP defines what a 404 means, not which addresses shelf has or which fields a book carries.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.
hint: The specification was renamed; the tools kept the old name.

pairs.right: the specification a description document follows
a tool that renders a document as an interactive page
the first line of a document in the old format
the first line of a document in the current format

right_distractors: the server that answers the requests a document describes

prompt: In this lesson's sense, what makes documentation "living"?
hint: Think about what happens the day the code changes and the document does not.

choices.text: It is generated from the code on every build
choices.why: Generation keeps it in step with what the code declares, and says nothing about what the code does, such as shelf's 501.

choices.text: Anybody can edit the page and see the change at once
choices.why: An editable page is still prose that nothing checks; it can be wrong and read perfectly.

choices.text: Its `info.version` is raised every time it changes
choices.why: That records that the description changed, not whether it is still true of the server.

choices.text: A test holds the running API up against it
choices.why: Right. The day the two disagree, the test fails, so the documentation cannot stay wrong quietly.

prompt: Under `responses`, a status code is written in quotes, as `"200"`, because the specification wants the keys as ___ and YAML would read a bare 200 as a number.
hint: Not a number.

prompt: In `$ref: "#/components/schemas/Book"`, what does the `#` stand for?
hint: Each segment after it is a key.

choices.text: The start of a YAML comment
choices.why: Inside quotes it is just a character of the string; a comment would have hidden the whole reference.

choices.text: The root of the same document
choices.why: Right. The pointer starts there and walks components, then schemas, then Book.

choices.text: The server's base address from `servers`
choices.why: References point inside documents, never at the running API.

choices.text: The first schema in the file, whatever its name
choices.why: A pointer is followed by name, key by key; position in the file plays no part.

prompt: Put the keys in order, from the outside in, on the way from `paths` to the schema of a JSON answer of `GET /books/{id}`.
hint: Address, then method, then what comes back.
trap: The status code sits above the media type: one code can have bodies in several media types.

prompt: How many operations does shelf's `openapi.yaml` describe?
hint: Count method and address pairs; `parameters` is not a method.

prompt: `rest.py` answers `DELETE /v1/books`, yet the document lists no `delete` under `/books`. Why?
hint: What does rest.py answer to it?

choices.text: The validator refuses a DELETE on a collection
choices.why: OpenAPI lets any method sit on any address; the choice was about what clients may rely on.

choices.text: Its only answer is a 405, so listing it would advertise an operation nobody can use
choices.why: Right. A document says what clients may rely on, and a method whose one answer is a refusal is not something to rely on.

choices.text: OpenAPI has no way to describe a 405
choices.why: A 405 can be listed like any other code; the document chose not to.

choices.text: HTTP forbids DELETE on a collection
choices.why: HTTP forbids nothing of the kind; shelf chose not to support it.

prompt: You fix a typo in the `summary` of `getBook`. Which number in the document should change?
hint: One of them is the version of the description itself.

choices.text: `openapi`, from 3.1.0 to 3.1.1
choices.why: That is the version of the specification the file follows, which did not change.

choices.text: The `/v1` at the end of the server's address
choices.why: That is the API's version, and a typo in a summary changes nothing a client sends or reads.

choices.text: `info.version`
choices.why: Right. It is the version of this description, and it moves whenever the description does.

choices.text: No number: a summary is not part of the document's content
choices.why: The summary is in the document and on the rendered page, so changing it changes the document.

prompt: Why did `pip install openapi-spec-validator==0.9.0` fail on Ubuntu 24.04 before the venv existed?
hint: Read the first line of the error.

choices.text: It needed sudo
choices.why: Root would not help; the refusal is about who manages the system's Python, not about permissions.

choices.text: The system's Python is marked as managed by apt
choices.why: Right. The error was `externally-managed-environment`, and its suggestion was a virtual environment.

choices.text: The VM could not reach the internet
choices.why: pip refused before downloading anything; the same command inside the venv downloaded fine.

choices.text: Version 0.9.0 does not support Python 3.12
choices.why: It installed and ran under the venv's Python 3.12 a moment later.

prompt: pip installed twenty packages for `openapi-spec-validator==0.9.0`. How many of those twenty had their version fixed by that `==0.9.0`?
hint: The pin names one package.

prompt: Which of these does `openapi-spec-validator` report? Choose all that apply.
hint: It reads the document and the rules of OpenAPI, and nothing else.

choices.text: A path `{author}` that no parameter declares
choices.why: Right. It printed `Path parameter 'author' ... was not resolved`.

choices.text: An ISBN pattern rest.py does not enforce
choices.why: The validator never sees rest.py; shelf's document passed with this rule in it.

choices.text: A `$ref` to a schema that does not exist
choices.why: Right. A pointer that lands nowhere is a broken document.

choices.text: A field the document promises and the server never sends
choices.why: Correct OpenAPI promising the wrong thing passes; only a test against the server finds it.

prompt: In code-first, what do people write by hand?
hint: The name says which comes first.

choices.text: The document, which the code is then built to match
choices.why: That is design-first.

choices.text: The code with annotations; the document is generated from it
choices.why: Right. FastAPI, springdoc, swag and the Node libraries all print the document from the code.

choices.text: Both, separately, and a test compares them
choices.why: That is what shelf has, and it is neither order: the document was written by hand after the code.

choices.text: Neither: a mock server produces both
choices.why: A mock server reads a document and answers with its examples; it writes neither.

prompt: A team generates its document with FastAPI. One handler raises an exception nobody expected, and the framework answers 500 with an HTML page. Does the generated document mention that answer?
hint: What does a generator read?

choices.text: Yes, because a framework documents every status it can produce
choices.why: It documents what handlers declare; an exception path is declared by nobody.

choices.text: Yes, as a `default` response added to every operation
choices.why: Nothing adds it on its own, and if somebody did, the 500 would become listed rather than found.

choices.text: No: it describes what the code declares, and a contract test is what would find the 500
choices.why: Right. The same happened to shelf's 501, which no handler wrote.

choices.text: Only if the generated document is committed to the repository
choices.why: Committing it makes changes visible in review; it cannot add an answer the generator never saw.

prompt: Match each situation to what it shows.
hint: Ask who wrote what first.

pairs.left: A front-end team builds against the contract before the back end exists
A rename in a model class changed the contract and nobody decided it should
The code stopped matching the agreed document and nothing noticed

pairs.right: written by hand, after the code

right_distractors: generated from rest.py on every build

prompt: The test created `9786500000085` as book 7, then `978-65-00000-08-5` as book 8. Why was the second not refused with a 409?
hint: What does the database compare?

choices.text: Book 7 had been deleted by then
choices.why: The deletes come after; book 7 still existed when book 8 was created.

choices.text: rest.py skips the uniqueness check on POST
choices.why: The second plain POST got its 409, so the check runs.

choices.text: `UNIQUE` compares strings, and the two strings differ
choices.why: Right. Same book, different text, so the database saw two ISBNs.

choices.text: The document's pattern switched the check off for hyphens
choices.why: rest.py never reads the document; nothing in it can switch anything off.

prompt: Put what `check_contract.py` does for one request in order.
hint: One check happens before anything is sent.
items: Check the body against the operation's `requestBody` schema
Look the status code up in `responses`
Validate the body against the response's schema
trap: The headers and the body of an answer can only be checked once the code says which response they belong to.

prompt: A contract test checks only the requests it ___, which is why `?author_id=abc` went unseen.
hint: What the test itself does with requests.

prompt: You add `check("GET", "/books?author_id=abc")` to `check_contract.py`. What does that line print?
hint: Which parts of a request does the script validate?

choices.text: `ok`: the script checks bodies, not query parameters, and `[]` fits the schema
choices.why: Right. The answer was 200 with an empty array, which is a valid list of books, so this check passes the very thing the section says it misses.

choices.text: FAIL, because the document says `author_id` is an integer
choices.why: That would need the script to validate parameters; it validates request bodies only.

choices.text: FAIL, because 200 is not listed for `GET /books`
choices.why: 200 is the one code `GET /books` does list.

choices.text: Nothing: `operation()` finds no template for a path with a query string
choices.why: It cuts the query string off before matching, which is how `?author_id=3` was checked.

prompt: You change `servers` to the VM's address and press Try it out in Swagger UI. Why is there still no answer from shelf?
hint: Where does rest.py listen?

choices.text: Swagger UI sends only GET requests
choices.why: Try it out sends whatever method the operation has.

choices.text: The document has no `securitySchemes`
choices.why: shelf needs no key; a missing scheme stops nothing.

choices.text: rest.py listens on 127.0.0.1 inside the VM, which nothing outside it reaches
choices.why: Right. Lesson 1 chose the loopback on purpose, and the course leaves it there.

choices.text: The VM's address changes on every request
choices.why: It is stable while the VM runs; `multipass info api` shows the same one each time.

prompt: What can Swagger UI do that Redoc does not?
hint: One of them is a reference to read.

choices.text: Read YAML as well as JSON
choices.why: Both read the same document in either spelling.

choices.text: Show the schemas behind each response
choices.why: Both lay out the schemas; it is the core of a reference page.

choices.text: Render the document without a browser
choices.why: Both are JavaScript that runs in a browser.

choices.text: Send real requests from the page
choices.why: Right. Try it out fills a form and sends it; Redoc only reads.

prompt: The top level says `security: [{staffKey: []}]` and `GET /books` says `security: []`. What does `GET /books` need?
hint: An operation's own list replaces the top-level one.

choices.text: The staff key, inherited from the top level
choices.why: Inheritance happens only when the operation says nothing; here it says something.

choices.text: Nothing: the empty list overrides the top level
choices.why: Right. That is how the list of books stays public while everything else needs the key.

choices.text: Any one of the schemes in `components`
choices.why: Defining a scheme makes it available; only a `security` list makes it required.

choices.text: Nothing, and no other operation can be called
choices.why: The empty list affects that operation alone.

prompt: Somebody adds an `apiKey` scheme to shelf's document and requires it on `POST /books`, and changes nothing else. A client posts a valid book with no key. What does it get?
hint: Who reads the document?

choices.text: 401, because the document now requires a key
choices.why: The document requires it on paper; rest.py never opens the document.

choices.text: 403, because the key is missing rather than wrong
choices.why: Neither code can come from a server that does not check keys.

choices.text: 201: describing a scheme enforces nothing
choices.why: Right. Only a contract test sending the request without a key would show the gap.

choices.text: A refusal from the validator before the request is sent
choices.why: The validator checks documents, not requests, and a client does not run it.

prompt: Match each security scheme `type` to what the client sends.
hint: Lessons 7, 8 and 9 build three of them.

pairs.right: a key in a header, a query string or a cookie
a token obtained through one of OAuth's flows
a certificate, during the TLS handshake

right_distractors: the session cookie the documentation page sets

prompt: What does a `default` response cost an operation's contract test?
hint: `default` means every code not listed.

choices.text: The test can no longer check a successful answer
choices.why: The listed codes, the 200 included, are checked as before.

choices.text: An unexpected 500 counts as listed, so a test honouring `default` passes it
choices.why: Right. A designed refusal and an accident look the same to it.

choices.text: The validator refuses a document that has one
choices.why: `default` is valid OpenAPI; the cost is in what it hides, not in validity.

choices.text: Every error body has to become `application/problem+json`
choices.why: `default` can carry any schema, shelf's `Error` among them.

prompt: Which of these changes to shelf's document is safe for existing clients?
hint: A request may accept more; a response may give more.

choices.text: Adding `stock` to the `required` list of `NewBook`
choices.why: A request now demands a field some clients never sent.

choices.text: Adding an optional `cover_url` to `NewBook`
choices.why: Right. The request accepts more, and a client that does not send it is unaffected.

choices.text: Removing `stock` from `Book`
choices.why: A response gives less, and a client reading the stock finds nothing.

choices.text: Requiring hyphens in the ISBN pattern of `NewBook`
choices.why: A request demands more, and every client sending thirteen plain digits is refused.

prompt: `diff` showed five changed lines after renaming `price_cents`. How many of them sit in schemas the client sends?
hint: `NewBook` and `BookChange` are sent; `Book` is received.

prompt: A new field `cover_url` is added to `Book` and also to its `required` list, and the server sends it on every book. A colleague says touching `required` is always breaking. Is this change breaking?
hint: Who reads `Book`?

choices.text: Yes: any change to `required` breaks clients
choices.why: That holds for a request; in a response, required means a promise the server keeps.

choices.text: Yes, because clients must now send `cover_url`
choices.why: Clients send `NewBook`, which did not change; `Book` is what they receive.

choices.text: No: in a response it is the server promising more
choices.why: Right. Readers that ignore the field are unaffected, and `Book` does not forbid extra fields.

choices.text: Only if the validator reports it
choices.why: The validator judges validity, and both versions are valid.

prompt: `operationId: createBook` is renamed to `addBook`; the HTTP behaviour does not change. What breaks?
hint: Where does a generated client take its names from?

choices.text: Every client calling `POST /v1/books`
choices.why: The request and the answer are what they were; a hand-written client notices nothing.

choices.text: Code built on a generated client, when it is regenerated
choices.why: Right. The function `createBook` disappears and every call to it stops compiling.

choices.text: The contract test, which looks operations up by id
choices.why: `check_contract.py` matches by method and path and never reads `operationId`.

choices.text: Nothing, since an `operationId` is only a label
choices.why: To a generator it is a function name, which makes it part of a contract.

prompt: Keep generated code in a directory of its own and never ___ it, because the next generation overwrites it.
hint: What you would otherwise do to fix something in it.

prompt: A pull request changes shelf's API and its document. Put the checks in the order they can run, cheapest first.
hint: Two of them need no server at all.
items: Compare it with the main branch's document for breaking changes
Start the server with the new code
Run the contract test against it
trap: Comparing a document that is not valid OpenAPI compares nothing reliable, so validity comes first.

prompt: Which of these tools send requests to a running server? Choose all that apply.
hint: Some only ever read files.

choices.text: `openapi-spec-validator`
choices.why: It reads the document and the rules of OpenAPI, nothing else.

choices.text: `check_contract.py`
choices.why: Right. Fifteen real requests, each answer compared with the document.

choices.text: Swagger UI's Try it out
choices.why: Right. It sends a real request from the browser, which is why it needs a server it can reach.

choices.text: A breaking-change checker such as oasdiff
choices.why: It compares two documents and never calls an API.

prompt: To make the contract test pass, a colleague adds a `default` error response to every operation of shelf's document. Does the OPTIONS line still fail?
hint: Which operation would that `default` belong to?

choices.text: No: the 501 now falls under `default`
choices.why: A `default` belongs to an operation, and the document has no `options` operation for it to sit in.

choices.text: Yes: the document still has no `options` operation
choices.why: Right. The test fails before it looks at any response; and `check_contract.py` ignores `default` anyway.

choices.text: No: `default` also covers methods the document does not list
choices.why: It covers status codes of one operation, never missing methods.

choices.text: It depends on whether the server is restarted
choices.why: The server never reads the document, so restarting it changes nothing here.

prompt: Which file should change to settle the ISBN disagreement, given what the document is for?
hint: The pattern is the shop's rule.

choices.text: `openapi.yaml`: drop the pattern so the two agree
choices.why: The test would pass and the shop's rule would be gone from the one place it was written.

choices.text: `check_contract.py`: stop sending the hyphenated ISBN
choices.why: The disagreement would still be there, now unwatched.

choices.text: `db.py`: add a CHECK on the column
choices.why: It would refuse the row, but a database error is not the 422 the document lists for a broken rule, and db.py only builds a new database.

choices.text: `rest.py`: check the pattern with the other field checks
choices.why: Right. The document states the rule, the code forgot it, and a 422 at the door is what the document promises.
